date.label: Undated Deuteronomic discourse and legislation
date.note: Biblical narrative chronology is not independently established as an absolute BCE date.

claims.claim: The firstfruits rite: when Israel enters the land, the offerer takes the first of all the fruit, puts it in a basket, and goes to the place the LORD chooses to place his name there (Deut 26:1–2), and the priest sets the basket before the altar (26:4).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:1–4, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The firstfruits confession recites: "A Syrian ready to perish was my father, and he went down into Egypt, and sojourned there with a few, and became there a nation, great, mighty, and populous" (Deut 26:5), through affliction, crying out, and deliverance "with a mighty hand, and with an outstretched arm" (26:6–9).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:5–9, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). The referent (Jacob) is Probable, stated in §3.1/§8.3, not in this claim.

claims.claim: The offerer rejoices "in every good thing which the LORD thy God hath given unto thee, and unto thine house, thou, and the Levite, and the stranger that is among you" (Deut 26:11).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:11, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: In the third year, the year of tithing, all the tithes of the increase are given to the Levite, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow, "that they may eat within thy gates, and be filled" (Deut 26:12).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:12, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The tithe declaration states the giver has brought away the hallowed things, given them as commanded, "not transgressed … neither have I forgotten," not eaten in mourning, not taken for unclean use, nor given for the dead (Deut 26:13–14).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:13–14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The tithe prayer asks the LORD to "look down from thy holy habitation, from heaven, and bless thy people Israel, and the land which thou hast given us" (Deut 26:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The mutual avowal: Israel avouches the LORD as God (26:17) and the LORD avouches Israel "to be his peculiar people" and "an holy people unto the LORD thy God" (26:18–19) — the same *sĕgullâ* language as Ex 19:5.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:16–19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). The *sĕgullâ* recurrence is a textual fact; no BDB gloss was consulted this session (§3.3).

claims.claim: Deut 26 closes the law corpus (Deut 12–26) and opens the covenant ceremony: the confessions presuppose settlement, and the avowal of vv. 16–19 is the transition to the Shechem ceremony of ch. 27.
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 26:16–19 (BibleGateway KJV) and the structure of chs. 26–27 as read. A structural judgment, not a textual fact.

claims.claim: On the day of crossing the Jordan, Israel is to set up great stones, plaster them, and write on them "all the words of this law" — "very plainly" (Deut 27:2–3, 8).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 27:2–3, 8, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The Masoretic Text of Deut 27:4 reads "in mount Ebal."
claims.evidence: Anderson & Giles, *The Samaritan Pentateuch*, pp. 53–54 (MT "Ebal" as the tradition).

claims.claim: The Samaritan Pentateuch reads "Gerizim" at Deut 27:4; 4QDeut-f has a lacuna at the place-name in v. 4 and attests neither reading; the Old Latin agrees with SP; whether Gerizim or Ebal is the earlier reading is disputed.
claims.evidence: Anderson & Giles, pp. 53–54, 169, read in part (searchable PDF passage; no full collation). Segal 2025 abstract only — the "Gerizim Composition" point is NOT verified for detailed argument. Full record: shared `deuteronomy-27-4-textual-criticism.md`.

claims.claim: The altar is built of whole stones, "thou shalt not lift up any iron tool upon them" (Deut 27:5–6); burnt and peace offerings are offered, eaten, and rejoiced over before the LORD (27:7).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 27:5–7, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: "Take heed, and hearken, O Israel; this day thou art become the people of the LORD thy God" (Deut 27:9), with the command to obey his voice and do his commandments (27:10).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 27:9–10, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Six tribes stand on Mount Gerizim to bless (Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, Benjamin) and six on Mount Ebal to curse (Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, Naphtali) (Deut 27:12–13).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 27:12–13, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The Levites pronounce twelve curses with a loud voice, and all the people answer "Amen" to each (Deut 27:14–26).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 27:14–26, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The two mountains were already named for blessing and curse before the crossing: "thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal" (Deut 11:29–30).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 11:29–30, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: Deut 28 is conditional both ways: "if thou shalt hearken diligently … all these blessings shall come on thee" (28:1–2); "if thou wilt not hearken … all these curses shall come upon thee" (28:15).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 28:1–2, 15, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The blessings (Deut 28:3–14) cover city and field, fruit of body/ground/cattle, basket and store, coming in and going out, victory over enemies, rain, lending without borrowing, and being "the head, and not the tail."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 28:3–14, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The curses of Deut 28:16–19 mirror the blessings of vv. 3–6 in inverted form (city/field, basket/store, fruit, coming in/going out).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 28:3–6, 16–19, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The first curse section (Deut 28:20–44) runs through disease (vv. 21–22, 27, 35), cosmic reversal (heaven brass, earth iron, v. 23; rain as dust, v. 24), defeat (v. 25), exposure of the dead (v. 26), madness and blindness (vv. 28–29), and the futility series (vv. 30–33, 38–42).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 28:20–44, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: The topic sequence of Deut 28:20–44 and EST §56 (the curse of the great gods) is, in Steymans' judgment, "almost identical" and unique, with parallel syntax (optative divine curses alternating with natural-force curses at parallel positions).
claims.evidence: Steymans, "Deuteronomy 28 and Tell Tayinat" (2013), read in part; ORACC SAA 2 no. 6 §56 (lines 472–493), read in full. The sequence parallel is documented; its explanation is Debated (see 022–023).

claims.claim: Steymans argues the Deut 28:20–44 / EST §56 similarities are due to direct borrowing from the EST, implying Deut 28:20–44 came into existence between 672 BCE and 622 BCE.
claims.evidence: Steymans 2013, abstract + article read in part (later tables/conclusion not reached). Presented as Steymans' argument, not as established fact.

claims.claim: Quick and Hutton/Crouch caution against a unique Vorlage and direct translation: Quick shows the futility-curse form is Northwest Semitic and Deuteronomy mediates East and West traditions; Hutton/Crouch (abstract only) find no procedural similarity to the Tell Fekheriyeh bilingual translation exemplar and argue reliance was unlikely to be limited to a single exemplar.
claims.evidence: Quick 2018, read in part (futility analysis + EST §§39–42 comparison read); Hutton & Crouch 2018, abstract only — NOT verified for detailed arguments.

claims.claim: The futility curse — maximum effort, minimal gain — is a standard Northwest Semitic literary form, attested in 43 biblical instances and 19 Old Aramaic instances (Sefire KAI 222, Tell Fakhariyah, Bukān; 9th–8th centuries BCE).
claims.evidence: Quick 2018, read in part; the counts and examples are Quick's, as read. The monograph (Quick 2017) was not read.

claims.claim: The Tell Tayinat exemplar of the EST (ms T-1808), found in 2009 in the inner sanctum of Building XVI, is a display tablet (40 × 26 cm, pierced for fixing); its §§54–55 invoke Levantine deities (Aramis of Qarnê, Adad/Sala of Kurba'il, Sarrat-Ekron, Bethel/Anat-Bethel, Kubaba of Carchemish).
claims.evidence: Steymans 2013, read in part (the Tayinat description and §§54–55 discussion). The Jerusalem-display inference is NOT in this claim — see §8.1.

claims.claim: The second curse section (Deut 28:45–68) raises the stakes: pursuit "till thou be destroyed" (v. 45), the yoke of iron (v. 48), a distant nation "whose tongue thou shalt not understand" (v. 49), siege (v. 52), scattering among all peoples (v. 64), and return to Egypt by ships (v. 68).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 28:45–68, read in full (BibleGateway KJV).

claims.claim: In the siege, the text states the eating of "the fruit of thine own body, the flesh of thy sons and of thy daughters" (Deut 28:53–57).
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 28:53–57, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Stated as text; presentation on the published page is Yonatan's decision (§8.4).

claims.claim: Deut 28:68 reverses the exodus: "the LORD shall bring thee into Egypt again with ships, by the way whereof I spake unto thee, Thou shalt see it no more again: and there ye shall be sold unto your enemies for bondmen and bondwomen, and no man shall buy you."
claims.evidence: KJV Deut 28:68, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). The "reversal" reading is Probable (stated in §3.1), not in this claim.

claims.claim: Leviticus 26 parallels Deut 28: blessings for obedience (Lev 26:3–13), escalating curses in four waves (vv. 14–39, including heaven as iron and earth as brass, v. 19; eating sons and daughters, v. 29; scattering, vv. 33–39), and a turn to confession and covenant remembrance (vv. 40–45) that Deut 28 lacks.
claims.evidence: Lev 26:1–46, read in full as a cross-reference (Leviticus KJV wording is outside the gateway entry’s Genesis/Exodus/Deuteronomy scope — not re-grounded onto it); KJV Deut 28, read in full (BibleGateway KJV). Parallel stated; no direction of dependence claimed.

claims.claim: There is no direct archaeological evidence for the Deut 27 Shechem ceremony (no inscription, plastered stones, or altar tied to it).
claims.evidence: §6.2 — the negative fact, stated as such; Historical Geography Report (provisional): "Deut 27 rite unverified by archaeology."

claims.claim: The Shechem landscape (two mountains flanking the valley) is geographically secure, matching Deut 27:12–13 and 11:29–30; the Deut 27 installations (where the stones and altar stood) are disputed.
claims.evidence: Historical Geography Report (provisional) for the landscape proposition; KJV Deut 27:12–13; 11:29–30, read in full (BibleGateway KJV) for the verse-matching element. No excavation report read directly — see §12.

claims.claim: The composition date of Deut 28 is not established: it follows from Steymans' direct borrowing only if that argument is accepted (672–622 BCE), and the cautionary position removes that terminus.
claims.evidence: Steymans 2013 (read in part); Quick 2018 (read in part); Hutton & Crouch 2018 (abstract only).

connections.note: Joshua builds the altar "in mount Ebal" (v. 30), whole stones, no iron (v. 31), writes the law on the stones (v. 32). Place-name follows MT.
"Half of them over against mount Gerizim, and half of them over against mount Ebal" (v. 33); the blessings and cursings read (v. 34).
"Thou shalt put the blessing upon mount Gerizim, and the curse upon mount Ebal" (11:29).
The unhewn-stone altar rule restated — the same rule as Ex 20:24–26.
The third-year tithe restated (Deut 14:28–29).
"Peculiar people" (*sĕgullâ*) — "a peculiar treasure … a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation" (Ex 19:5–6).
Firstfruits: the sheaf waved before the LORD (Lev 23:10–14).
Blessings for obedience in both chapters (Lev 26) (rain, increase, peace, victory).
First curse waves in both (Lev 26) (terror, consumption, heaven as iron/earth as brass, strength spent in vain, bread by weight).
Escalation and scattering in both (Lev 26) (sevenfold chastisement, desolation, scattering among the heathen).
"Ye shall eat the flesh of your sons, and the flesh of your daughters shall ye eat" (Lev 26:29). Single-verse target, split from conn-deu-07-010's range.
"The hands of the pitiful women have sodden their own children" in the siege of Jerusalem (Lam 4:10).
(2 Kgs 25:1–3) The siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar; "the famine prevailed in the city" (v. 3).
"The LORD shall scatter you among the nations … and there ye shall serve gods, the work of men's hands, wood and stone" (Deut 4:27–28).
"Israel shall be a proverb and a byword among all people" (1 Kgs 9:7–8).
"Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the law to do them" (Gal 3:10–14, quoting Deut 27:26).
"The carcases of this people shall be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth" (Jer 7:33).
Serving "gods, the work of men's hands, wood and stone" (Deut 4:28).
"I have set before thee this day life and good, and death and evil" (Deut 30:15) — the blessing/curse choice restated in the renewal. Cross-category (Cat. 8).
"All the curses that are written in this book shall lie upon him" (Deut 29:20). Cross-category (Cat. 8).
